title: Scope: the decidable, finitely-searchable core of OQ-05
content: The module docstring is unusually careful about what is and is not claimed. Erdős #1012's fifth open question asks for the computational complexity of detecting an (n−k)-cycle in a graph with T(n,k)−1 edges — a question whose full answer (a polynomial algorithm, or an NP-hardness reduction) is out of reach of current Mathlib. This file instead pins down the honest computational core the question presupposes: for a fixed finite graph, cycle detection is Decidable (a decision procedure provably exists), it is realised by an explicit finite brute-force search, and that search space has exactly |V|^ℓ candidates. The docstring's explicit 'What This File Does NOT Claim' section stresses that the |V|^ℓ bound is exponential and no hardness result is proved — the file delimits the decidable skeleton on which any future complexity analysis rests. Setup: import Mathlib and the parent Erdos1012Problem, namespace Erdos1012OQ05, open Erdos1012, and a fixed finite decidable-eq vertex type V.
mathContext: For fixed finite $G$: 'contains an $\ell$-cycle' is $\mathrm{Decidable}$, equivalent to a search over $\{c : \mathrm{Fin}\,\ell \to V\}$ of size $|V|^{\ell}$.

title: The ℓ = 0 Base Case: No Cycle Has Length Zero
content: `not_hasCycleOfLength_zero` records the recursion's base case: a cycle of length `0` cannot exist, since `hasCycleOfLength G 0` unfolds (via `simp [hasCycleOfLength]`) to a claim about an injective closed walk on the empty index type `Fin 0`, which is vacuously unsatisfiable in the form required. This is exactly the fact the `ℓ = 0` branch of `decidableHasCycleOfLength` leans on when it returns `decidable_of_iff False`. Small as it is, it anchors the well-founded definition: every decidability and search-space statement below is a statement about the `l + 1` successor case, with this providing the floor.
mathContext: A cycle has at least three distinct vertices; in particular there is no cycle of length $0$, so $\neg\,\mathrm{hasCycleOfLength}\,G\,0$ holds for every graph $G$.

title: Cycle Detection is Decidable — an Executable Procedure Exists
content: `decidableHasCycleOfLength` is the computational heart of this entry. `hasCycleOfLength G (l+1)` is an existential `∃ c : Fin (l+1) → V, Injective c ∧ (closed-walk condition)`. Three facts make it decidable: the domain `Fin (l+1) → V` is a `Fintype`; injectivity of a finite-domain map is decidable (`Fintype.decidableInjectiveFintype`, needing `DecidableEq V`); and the adjacency condition is a decidable bounded `∀` (needing `DecidableRel G.Adj`). `Fintype.decidableExistsFintype` then bundles them. The `ℓ = 0` case reduces to `False`. This turns 'does G contain an (n−k)-cycle?' from a bare proposition into a question an algorithm answers.
mathContext: A predicate $\exists c \in F,\, P(c)$ with $F$ finite and $P$ decidable is itself decidable, by exhaustive search over $F$.

title: Decidability Propagates to Hamiltonicity and Pancyclicity
content: Once cycle-length detection is decidable, the natural derived graph predicates inherit it for free. `decidableIsHamiltonian` observes that Hamiltonicity is just `hasCycleOfLength G |V|` — a single instance of the core predicate — so it reuses `decidableHasCycleOfLength` directly. Pancyclicity needs one reformulation first: `isPancyclicUpTo_iff` rewrites `isPancyclicUpTo G m` as the bounded conjunction `∀ l ∈ Finset.Icc 3 m, hasCycleOfLength G l`, a finite `∀` over a decidable family; `decidableIsPancyclicUpTo` then transports decidability across that equivalence with `decidable_of_iff`. The pattern is the workhorse of computable mathematics: express each new predicate as a `Fintype`-bounded quantifier over an already-decidable one, and its decision procedure assembles automatically.
mathContext: $G$ is Hamiltonian iff it has a cycle of length $|V|$; $G$ is pancyclic up to $m$ iff it has a cycle of every length $\ell \in [3,m]$ — each a finite combination of decidable cycle-length tests, hence decidable.

title: The Brute-Force Search Space is Exactly |V|^ℓ
content: `hasCycleOfLength_iff_exists_mem_univ` spells the decision procedure out as a literal search over the finite universe of candidate vertex sequences `Fin ℓ → V`, and `searchSpace_card` counts that universe: `Fintype.card (Fin ℓ → V) = |V|^ℓ` (via `Fintype.card_fun` and `Fintype.card_fin`). Specialized to a Hamiltonian cycle, `hamiltonianSearchSpace_card` gives `n^n`. This is the explicit — and exponential — cost of the naive algorithm. It is deliberately *not* a polynomial bound: whether the restricted instances at `T(n,k)−1` edges admit anything faster is exactly the open part of OQ-05.
mathContext: $|\{c : \mathrm{Fin}\,\ell \to V\}| = |V|^{\ell}$; the Hamiltonian search space on $n$ vertices has $n^n$ candidate sequences.

title: The Procedure Actually Runs (via `decide`, not `native_decide`)
content: Because the decidability instance is computable, `decide` evaluates concrete cases in the kernel: `triangle_has_3cycle` confirms K₃ has a 3-cycle, while `edgeless_no_3cycle` and `edgeless_not_hamiltonian_fin3` confirm the empty graph on three vertices has neither. These use `decide` (kernel reduction of the `Decidable` instance), *not* `native_decide` — so no `Lean.ofReduceBool` is introduced and the entry stays genuinely 0-axiom. They demonstrate the formalized decision problem is executable, not merely classically decidable.
mathContext: The complete graph $K_3$ is a single triangle, hence a 3-cycle; the edgeless graph has no edges and so no cycle of any length.
